clinicalPearls: A sight-threatening complication of pathological (degenerative) myopia driven by progressive axial elongation of the globe and formation of a posterior staphyloma

The META-PM classification grades categories from tessellated fundus through diffuse and patchy chorioretinal atrophy to macular atrophy, with three 'plus' lesions: lacquer cracks, myopic choroidal neovascularisation and Fuchs spot
Lacquer cracks are breaks in Bruch's membrane that predispose to myopic choroidal neovascularisation and subretinal haemorrhage
Myopic choroidal neovascularisation is typically small, grey and subfoveal or juxtafoveal and may leave a pigmented scar (Fuchs or Forster-Fuchs spot); anti-VEGF therapy is the mainstay of treatment
Myopic traction maculopathy, including foveoschisis, results from inward traction on a stretched, non-compliant retina overlying a staphyloma and may progress to macular hole and detachment
Dome-shaped macula and peripapillary changes such as myopic conus, peripapillary atrophy and tilted disc are recognised associated features that can complicate glaucoma assessment
OCT is essential for detecting neovascularisation, foveoschisis, macular hole and dome-shaped macula, and OCT-angiography aids detection of myopic choroidal neovascularisation
Because early myopic neovascularisation is very treatable, patients benefit from education about warning symptoms and often Amsler grid monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Pathological myopia is characterised by excessive axial elongation of the eye and development of a posterior staphyloma, an outpouching of the wall of the globe. Progressive mechanical stretching thins the retina, retinal pigment epithelium, Bruch's membrane and choroid, producing chorioretinal atrophy and breaks in Bruch's membrane known as lacquer cracks. These breaks together with the attenuated choroid predispose to myopic choroidal neovascularisation and subsequent scarring (Fuchs spot). Over the rigid, non-compliant posterior pole, persistent vitreoretinal and epiretinal traction on a stretched retina causes myopic traction maculopathy and foveoschisis, which may progress to full-thickness macular hole and retinal detachment. The combination of atrophy, neovascularisation and traction accounts for the central visual loss.
additionalDifferentials: Choroidal neovascularisation of inflammatory or idiopathic origin
Macular hole or vitreomacular traction of other aetiology
Tilted disc syndrome with associated maculopathy
Punctate inner choroidopathy and other inflammatory chorioretinopathies in young myopes
additionalInvestigations: OCT of the macula for neovascularisation, foveoschisis, macular hole and dome-shaped macula
OCT-angiography and/or fundus fluorescein angiography to detect and characterise myopic choroidal neovascularisation
Fundus autofluorescence and colour imaging to map chorioretinal atrophy and lacquer cracks
Measurement of axial length and refraction to confirm the degree of myopia
Wide-field imaging and peripheral retinal examination, as high myopes are also at risk of peripheral breaks and detachment
redFlags: New metamorphopsia, a central scotoma or sudden drop in central vision suggesting neovascularisation or subretinal haemorrhage
Flashes, floaters or a field defect suggesting retinal detachment, to which high myopes are predisposed
Progressive distortion suggesting foveoschisis advancing towards a macular hole
Fresh subretinal haemorrhage at the fovea
reference.prognosis: Myopic maculopathy is a leading cause of irreversible central visual impairment in high myopia and tends to progress with age and increasing axial length. Nonetheless, early detection and prompt anti-VEGF treatment of myopic choroidal neovascularisation gives a relatively favourable visual outcome compared with untreated disease.
pitfalls: Attributing reduced vision solely to refractive error and missing treatable myopic choroidal neovascularisation
Misinterpreting myopic disc and peripapillary changes, leading to over- or under-diagnosis of glaucoma
Overlooking foveoschisis on clinical examination when OCT would reveal it
Failing to examine the peripheral retina for breaks in a high myope
Confusing myopic neovascularisation with neovascular AMD, which differs in lesion size, behaviour and treatment response
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
International photographic classification and grading system for myopic maculopathy (META-PM)
management: Treat myopic choroidal neovascularisation promptly with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections as the mainstay of therapy
Consider vitreoretinal surgery, such as vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peeling, for myopic traction maculopathy, foveoschisis and macular hole
Repair associated retinal detachment surgically and treat peripheral retinal breaks
Monitor with serial optical coherence tomography and OCT-angiography, and provide an Amsler grid for symptom self-monitoring
Optimise refractive correction and provide low-vision aids and rehabilitation for irreversible central visual loss
Surveil for and manage coexisting glaucoma, allowing for the difficult optic disc assessment in high myopia
Refer to medical retina and advise prompt review of any new distortion or scotoma
